[Generalized Linear Models]{.custom-title}




[Grayson White]{.custom-subtitle} [Stat 243
Fall 2026, Week 12]{.custom-subtitle} ::: ::::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Announcements ::: {.nonincremental} - Lab 9 released. Due 12/4. - Lab 10 to be released 12/4, covering Week 12 and 13 content (GLMs and LMMs). ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Two models **Linear Regression:** \begin{align*} y_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi} + \epsilon_i \\ \epsilon_i &\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2) \end{align*}
**Logistic Regression:** $$ \log \left( \frac{P(y_i = 1)}{1 - P(y_i = 1)} \right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi} $$ $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Bern(p_i), \textrm{where}~p_i = P(y_i = 1) $$ # Both Logistic and Linear Regression can be written as **Generalized Linear Models** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) A generalized linear model has three components: 1. A distribution of $y_i$ 2. A link function, $g(\mu_i)$, where $\mu_i = \mathbb{E}(y_i)$ 3. Linear predictor, $\eta_i$ ::: {.fragment} A GLM is written as follows: $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Dist(g^{-1}(\eta_i)) $$ where: ::: {.nonincremental} - $Dist$ is the assumed distribution of $y_i$, - $g^{-1}(\eta_i)$ is the value of the inverse link, which is $\mu_i$, and - $\eta_i$ is the linear predictor. ::: ::: ## Logistic regression fully specified as a GLM **Logistic Regression:** $$ \log \left( \frac{P(y_i = 1)}{1 - P(y_i = 1)} \right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi} $$ $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Bern(p_i), \textrm{where}~p_i = P(y_i = 1) $$ ::: {.fragment} **Logistic Regression (as a GLM):** $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Bern\left(\frac{\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})}{1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})}\right) $$ ::: 1. Distribution of $y_i$: Bernoulli 2. Link function: logit; $g(p_i) = \log\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, so $p_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \frac{\exp(\eta_i)}{1 + \exp(\eta_i)}$ 3. Linear predictor: $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ ## Assumptions for logistic regression Now that we have written down the logistic regression model, $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Bern\left(\frac{\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})}{1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})}\right), $$ we can see its assumptions: 1. **Binary Response:** The response variable is dichotomous (two possible responses). 2. **Independence:** The observations must be independent of one another. 3. **Variance Structure:** By definition, the variance of a Bernoulli random variable is $p(1−p)$, so that variability is highest when $p=.5$. 4. **Linearity:** The log odds, $\log\left(\frac{p}{1−p}\right)$, must be a linear function of $x$. ## Your turn: Write the linear regression model as a GLM **Linear Regression:** \begin{align*} y_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi} + \epsilon_i \\ \epsilon_i &\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2) \end{align*} ::: {.fragment} **Linear Regression (as a GLM):** $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi},~ \sigma^2) $$ ::: 1. Distribution of $y_i$: Normal 2. Link function: identity; $g(\mu_i) = \mu_i$, so $\mu_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \eta_i$ 3. Linear predictor: $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
05:00
``` ::: ::: ## Consider - Why is it important that we use the link function $g(p_i) = \log\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$ for logistic regression? - Why is it okay that we use the identity link in linear regression? ## Probit regression Consider the following GLM: 1. Distribution of $y_i$: Bernoulli 2. Link function: "probit"; - $g(p_i) = \Phi^{-1}(p_i)$, so $p_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \Phi(\eta_i)$, - where $\Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{z} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-t^2/2} \, dt$ is the standard normal CDF 3. Linear predictor: $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$
::: {.fragment} **Probit regression as a GLM:** $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Bern(\Phi(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})) $$ ::: ## Probit regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(forested) mod_logit <- glm( formula = forested ~ canopy_cover, data = forested, family = binomial(link = "logit") ) mod_probit <- glm( formula = forested ~ canopy_cover, data = forested, family = binomial(link = "probit") ) coef(mod_logit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) canopy_cover 2.22962905 -0.08723057 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coef(mod_probit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) canopy_cover 1.28704549 -0.04734969 ``` ::: ::: - Note: `family = "binomial"` gives you a logit link function by default. ## Plotting probit regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} forested %>% mutate(z = ifelse(forested == "Yes", 1, 0)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = canopy_cover, y = z)) + geom_jitter(height = 0.03, width = 0, alpha = 0.15) + geom_smooth(method = "glm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue", method.args = list(family = binomial(link = "logit"))) + geom_smooth(method = "glm", se = FALSE, color = "goldenrod", method.args = list(family = binomial(link = "probit"))) + labs(x = "Percent canopy cover", y = "P(forested)") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: # A GLM for Count Data ## Current Distributional Options The Normal and Bernoulli distributions are as follows: ::: {.nonincremental} $Y \sim Normal(\mu, \sigma^2)$: $$ f(y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \text{ for } y \in \mathbb{R}. $$ $Y\sim Bernoulli(p)$: $$ P(Y = y) = p^y (1 - p)^{1 - y}, \text{ for } y \in \{0, 1\}. $$ ::: ::: {.fragment} What if our response variable is a **count**, i.e., $y \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$? ::: ::: {.fragment} $Y\sim Poisson(\lambda)$: $$ P(Y = y) = \frac{\lambda^y e^{-\lambda}}{y!}, \text{ for } y \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}. $$ ::: ## Poisson Distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame(x = c(0:10), y = dpois(0:10, lambda = 1)) %>% ggplot(mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + labs(title = latex2exp::TeX("$Y \\sim Pois(\\lambda = 1)$"), x = "y", y = "P(Y = y)") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Poisson Distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame(x = c(0:20), y = dpois(0:20, lambda = 5)) %>% ggplot(mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + labs(title = latex2exp::TeX("$Y \\sim Pois(\\lambda = 5)$"), x = "y", y = "P(Y = y)") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Poisson Distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame(x = c(0:50), y = dpois(0:50, lambda = 20)) %>% ggplot(mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + labs(title = latex2exp::TeX("$Y \\sim Pois(\\lambda = 20)$"), x = "y", y = "P(Y = y)") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## How can we construct a GLM for counts based on the Poisson distribution? ::: {.fragment} Remember, a GLM consists of three components: ::: {.nonincremental} 1. A distribution of $y_i$ 2. A link function, $g(\mu_i)$, where $\mu_i = \mathbb{E}(y_i)$ 3. Linear predictor, $\eta_i$ ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
05:00
``` ::: ::: ## Poisson regression as a GLM 1. Distribution of $y_i$: Poisson 2. Link function: log; $g(\lambda_i) = \log(\lambda_i)$, so $\lambda_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \exp(\eta_i)$ 3. Linear predictor: $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ ::: {.fragment} $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Pois\left(\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})\right) $$ :::

::: {.fragment .fade-up .midi .center} (**Boardwork**) A graphical comparison of Normal and Poisson regression. ::: ## A graphical comparison of Normal and Poisson regression ![](img/OLSpois-1.png){width='70%' fig-align='center'} ## Poisson regression assumptions Now that we have written down the Poisson regression model, $$ y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} Pois\left(\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})\right) $$ we can see its assumptions: 1. **Poisson Response:** The response variable is a count, described by a Poisson distribution. 2. **Independence:** The observations must be independent of one another. 3. **Mean = Variance:** By definition, the mean of a Poisson random variable must be equal to its variance. 4. **Linearity:** The log of the mean rate, $\log(\lambda)$, must be a linear function of $x$. ## Poisson regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/proback/BeyondMLR/master/data/fHH1.csv") head(household) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 6 ...1 location age total numLT5 roof 1 1 CentralLuzon 65 0 0 Predominantly Strong Material 2 2 MetroManila 75 3 0 Predominantly Strong Material 3 3 DavaoRegion 54 4 0 Predominantly Strong Material 4 4 Visayas 49 3 0 Predominantly Strong Material 5 5 MetroManila 74 3 0 Predominantly Strong Material 6 6 Visayas 59 6 0 Predominantly Strong Material ``` ::: ::: - Data on households in the Philippines (more info: [Chapter 4.4 of Beyond MLR](https://bookdown.org/roback/bookdown-BeyondMLR/ch-poissonreg.html)) - Each row represents a household - `age` = the age of the head of household - `total` = the number of people in the household other than the head ## Exploratory data analysis ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = household, mapping = aes(x = total)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Poisson regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_pois <- glm( formula = total ~ age, data = household, family = poisson(link = "log") ) broom::tidy(mod_pois) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 1.55 0.0503 30.8 1.07e-208 2 age -0.00471 0.000936 -5.03 5.01e- 7 ``` ::: ::: ## Plotting Poisson regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "glm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue", method.args = list(family = poisson(link = "log"))) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Plotting Poisson vs linear regression ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} household %>% ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "glm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue", method.args = list(family = poisson(link = "log"))) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "tomato", linetype = "dashed") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk12mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: Linear regression produces nearly the same line. Advantages of Poisson regression? ## Next time ::: {.nonincremental} - More fun with GLMs :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
